title: Volume of Prisms: Rectangular and Triangular Prisms
seo_title: Year 7 Volume of Prisms Worksheets: Rectangular and Triangular Prisms (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: solve problems involving the volume of right prisms including rectangular and triangular prisms, using established formulas and appropriate units
meta_desc: Free Year 7 maths worksheets on the volume of prisms for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M7M02): rectangular prisms, missing dimensions, triangular prisms, area of cross-section × length and practical problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length.
key_sub: For a triangular prism, find the triangle's area first (½ × base × height).
body_html:
How it works

A right prism has the same cross-section all the way through. Volume = area of cross-section × length.

For a rectangular prism this is length × width × height. For a triangular prism, first find the area of the triangle (½ × base × height), then multiply by the length. Volume is measured in cubic units such as cm³ and m³.

Example

Find the volume of the rectangular prism above.

5 × 3 × 4.

Answer: 60 cm³

Example

A triangular prism has a right-angled triangle 6 cm by 8 cm and length 10 cm.

Triangle area = ½ × 6 × 8 = 24 cm².

24 × 10 = 240.

Answer: 240 cm³

Common mistakes

  • Adding the lengths instead of multiplying.
  • Forgetting to halve when the cross-section is a triangle.
  • Halving twice when the cross-section area is already given.
  • Writing cm² instead of cm³ for a volume.

faq.q: How do I find the volume of a rectangular prism?
faq.a: Multiply length × width × height. A 5 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm prism has volume 60 cm³.

faq.q: How do I find the volume of a triangular prism?
faq.a: Find the area of the triangular end (½ × base × height), then multiply by the length of the prism.
A 3-D shape with the same cross-section all the way through, whose sides meet the ends at right angles.

faq.q: How do I find a missing height?
faq.a: Divide the volume by the area of the base. 112 cm³ ÷ 16 cm² = 7 cm.
